newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil oil law seen bolstering Petrobras.
newsitem.headline: Brazil oil law seen bolstering Petrobras.

text.p: Petrobras, Brazil's state-owned energy giant, is set to remain the dominant player in the country's oil and gas sectors once a bill regulating the end of its monopoly is approved, deputies and analysts said.

A draft version of the bill, which was given a first reading in a Chamber of Deputies commitee last week, lays down rules for how Petrobras and private companies may compete or create joint ventures to develop Brazil's energy wealth.

"Petrobas has been a monopoly for 40 years, it has data that no others have and it will compete with all its strength. Over time there will be a gradual leveling of the playing field," said deputy Eliseu Resende who drew up the bill.

Shares in Petrobras soared last week after Resende said his bill would drop existing restrictions on foreigners buying the company's voting shares and on expectations Petrobras would do well out of the upcoming legislation.
Brazil's Congress voted in 1995 to end the state's monopoly on oil and gas but has not yet appproved the enabling legislation to put that decision into practice.

Brazilian oil production is expected to reach 900,000 barrels per day in 1997 but demand will also grow to 1.5 million bpd, putting pressure on Brazil's worrisome trade deficit and spurring the government to seek quick approval of the bill.
The centerpiece of the new law is the creation of a National Petroleum Agency (ANP), a regulator which will effectively decide who gets what of Brazil's gas and oil reserves.

The bill allows Petrobras to maintain areas where it is already producing or involved in exploration work and gives it three months after approval of the new law to inform the ANP which areas it wants to keep.

Wagner Freire, a consultant and a former Petrobras director, said the size of Petrobras' dominance in the future would depend on how the ANP interprets criteria in the bill for defining which areas under exploration the state giant may maintain.

The law says Petrobras can keep areas for which it has drawn up an exploration plan and which it can afford to develop, a clause which could lead to political interference because Petrobras' budget is set by the government, Freire said.

Private companies would probably be reluctant to compete with Petrobras because the most promising areas would be under its control. "If good areas become available, they will want to bid for them themselves. If not, they will have to associate with Petrobras," Freire said.

He said he hoped Congress would change other clauses included in the bill that might stifle competition, including a rule that natural gas producers may not sell directly to industrial consumers but instead use local distributors.

Roberto Lima Neto, a pro-privatization deputy, said the bill would further strengthen Petrobras by allowing it to strike up joint ventures without congressional approval, giving it a wealth of options to maintain its grip on the sector.
"We could end up with Petrobras still in charge of the monopoly but with a lot more money behind it," Lima Neto said.
